newsitem.title: ITALY: Hard-left wants probe into Italy role in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Hard-left wants probe into Italy role in Albania.

text.p: Italy's communist party called on Wednesday for an inquiry into Italian diplomatic and financial involvement in Albania, alleging that suspect dealings may have contributed to the Balkan country's slide into anarchy.

The Communist Refoundation party, uneasy allies of Rome's centre-left government, put forward a draft law in the lower Chamber of Deputies calling for a parliamentary commission to be set up to probe Italy's role in Albania.

Though it was not clear when the draft would be debated, the submission in itself was potentially embarrassing to the government, which has taken the lead in international efforts to restore order in its impoverished Adriatic neighbour.

The step could also raise fresh tensions within Italy's centre-left coalition, which was almost toppled in April when Refoundation refused to support the deployment of an Italian-led multinational military force in Albania.
The Refoundation proposal was signed by six deputies including the party's lower house leader, Oliviero Diliberto.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini had no substantive comment on the proposal, saying it was up to parliament to examine it.

Parts of Albania -- especially in the south -- are effectively out of government control after a wave of violence and chaos was unleashed by popular outrage at the collapse of fraudulent pyramid savings schemes early this year.

Insurgents have blamed the penury resulting from the crash on President Sali Berisha, who agreed under international pressure in March to set up a national unity government to lead Albania to early general elections, due on June 29.
The Refoundation proposal said the crisis in Albania had not come as a "bolt from the blue" but was the result of political and economic developments in which Italy had had a hand.

The collapse of the savings schemes and other factors, including alleged fraud in elections in 1996 that won Berisha's Democratic Party a landslide, "represent a collection of facts that cast a worrying shadow over the role played by our country", a statement accompanying the draft law said.
It said issues the proposed inquiry should examine included:
-- whether Italian banks and credit institutes were involved in the Albanian savings schemes and whether the schemes were infiltrated by organised crime.
-- why an Italian intelligence report to parliament on the situation in Albania had apparently failed to remark on Albania's mounting unrest.
-- allegations from 1996 foreign election observers that they had faced Italian pressure to tone down their reports of ballot rigging.
"Parliament needs to understand whether the Italian government simply underestimated the extent of electoral fraud or was purposely trying to cover it up," Refoundation said.
Italy, which has close economic links with Albania and has struggled to contain an influx of illegal Albanian immigrants, was long regarded as a staunch ally of Berisha.
It has distanced itself from the rightist president since this year's unrest and has identified Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, an opposition Socialist, as its main point of contact.
Italy's outgoing ambassador to Albania Paolo Foresti, who took up a new post in Brussels on Wednesday, left Tirana amid controversy over alleged bias in favour of Berisha.
His replacement has been named as Marcello Spatafora after another designated successor was relieved of the appointment 48 hours after being nominated for public criticism of Foresti.
